guide.summary: Calculus-based kinematics describes motion with derivatives and integrals: v = dx/dt, a = dv/dt, and their integrals, including motion with non-constant acceleration, graphical analysis, two-dimensional and projectile motion, and relative velocity.

sections.heading: Calculus of motion
sections.body: Velocity is the time derivative of position, v = dx/dt; acceleration is the derivative of velocity, a = dv/dt = d²x/dt². Going backward, Δx = ∫v dt and Δv = ∫a dt; include initial conditions to find constants. The constant-acceleration equations are special cases. When acceleration depends on position, use a = v dv/dx and integrate ∫v dv = ∫a dx. When it depends on velocity, separate variables: dv/a(v) = dt. An object speeds up when v and a have the same sign and slows down when they have opposite signs. Displacement can be zero while distance traveled is not; find turning points where v = 0.

sections.heading: Graphs
sections.body: On an x–t graph, slope = velocity; on a v–t graph, slope = acceleration and area = displacement; on an a–t graph, area = change in velocity. Curvature of an x–t graph indicates acceleration: concave up means a > 0.

sections.heading: Two dimensions and projectiles
sections.body: Treat x and y motion independently with vectors r(t), v(t) = dr/dt, a(t) = dv/dt. For a projectile (no air resistance), a_x = 0 and a_y = −g. Launch at speed v₀ and angle θ from level ground: time of flight 2v₀ sin θ/g, maximum height (v₀ sin θ)²/2g, range v₀² sin 2θ/g (maximum at 45°). Relative velocity: v_A/C = v_A/B + v_B/C.

sections.heading: Worked example: calculus kinematics
sections.body: A particle moves with velocity v(t) = 3t² − 12t + 9 m/s. Its acceleration is a(t) = 6t − 12, and it is momentarily at rest when v = 0, at t = 1 s and t = 3 s. If x(0) = 2 m, position is x(t) = t³ − 6t² + 9t + 2. Displacement from t = 0 to 3 s is x(3) − x(0) = 0, but distance traveled is |x(1) − x(0)| + |x(3) − x(1)| = 4 + 4 = 8 m, because the particle reverses direction at t = 1 s. Distance requires splitting the integral of speed where velocity changes sign.

sections.heading: Worked example: projectile motion
sections.body: A ball is launched at 20 m/s at 30° above horizontal from level ground. The components are vx = 20 cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m/s and vy = 10 m/s. Using g = 9.8 m/s², time to the peak is 10/9.8 ≈ 1.02 s, total flight time about 2.04 s, maximum height (10)²/(2 × 9.8) ≈ 5.1 m, and range about 17.3 × 2.04 ≈ 35.3 m. Horizontal velocity is constant, and vertical acceleration is −g throughout the flight.

sections.heading: Worked example: variable acceleration
sections.body: If acceleration depends on velocity, such as a = −kv, separate variables: dv/v = −k dt, giving v(t) = v₀e^(−kt). Integrating again gives position x(t) = (v₀/k)(1 − e^(−kt)), which approaches v₀/k as t → ∞. This approach also appears in resistive force problems in Unit 2.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students confuse displacement with distance, forget initial conditions when integrating, and treat acceleration as constant when it varies. Always check whether constant-acceleration equations apply before using them.

sections.heading: Exam connection
sections.body: Free-response questions ask you to derive expressions, sketch graphs of position, velocity, and acceleration, and connect slopes and areas of graphs to physical quantities.

sections.heading: Laboratory and experimental design
sections.body: To measure acceleration, use a motion sensor or video analysis to record position versus time, then fit a quadratic curve or graph velocity versus time and find the slope. Linearizing data, for example graphing displacement against t² for an object starting from rest, gives a line with slope a/2. Report uncertainty and discuss sources of error such as friction and timing.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body: v = dx/dt; a = dv/dt; x = ∫v dt; v = ∫a dt; constant acceleration: v = v₀ + at, x = x₀ + v₀t + ½at², v² = v₀² + 2aΔx.

sections.heading: Derivation tips
sections.body: Start derivations from definitions, not memorized formulas.

sections.heading: Graph skills
sections.body: Slopes and areas of motion graphs carry meaning.

keyTakeaways: v = dx/dt, a = dv/dt; integrate with initial conditions.
a = v dv/dx for position-dependent acceleration.
Speeding up: v and a same sign.
Projectile: independent x and y; a_y = −g.
commonMistakes: Using constant-acceleration equations when a varies.
Forgetting the constant of integration (initial position or velocity).
Confusing distance with displacement when the object reverses.
Saying an object slows down whenever acceleration is negative.
Treating the vertical velocity at the top of a projectile's path as the full velocity.
examTips: Show the integral or derivative explicitly; FRQ points require the calculus step.
For distance, split the interval at each turning point.
Graph-translation questions: match slopes and areas between x, v, a graphs.
For drag-type problems, write the differential equation before solving.
guide.cramSheet:

**Integrals:** Δx = ∫v dt · Δv = ∫a dt · +initial conditions

**Tricks:** a = v dv/dx · separate variables for a(v)

**Speed:** up if v, a same sign

**Graphs:** x–t slope v · v–t slope a, area Δx · a–t area Δv

**Projectile:** a_x = 0 · a_y = −g · R = v₀² sin 2θ/g · H = (v₀ sin θ)²/2g

practice.prompt: A particle moves along the x-axis with acceleration a(t) = 12 − 6t (m/s², t in seconds). At t = 0, v = −9 m/s and x = 0.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Starting from the definition of acceleration, derive an expression for v(t).

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Determine the times when the particle is momentarily at rest, and state the direction of motion during 0 < t < 1 s and 1 s < t < 3 s.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Determine x(t) and calculate the position at t = 3 s.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Calculate the total distance traveled from t = 0 to t = 3 s.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: At t = 0.5 s, is the particle speeding up or slowing down? Justify.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. a = dv/dt, so v = ∫(12 − 6t) dt = 12t − 3t² + C. At t = 0, v = −9 m/s, so C = −9. v(t) = −9 + 12t − 3t² m/s.

B. v = 0 → −3(t² − 4t + 3) = −3(t − 1)(t − 3) = 0 → t = 1 s and t = 3 s. For 0 < t < 1, v is negative (e.g., v(0.5) = −3.75), so the particle moves in the −x direction. For 1 < t < 3, v is positive (e.g., v(2) = 3), so it moves in the +x direction.

C. x = ∫v dt = −9t + 6t² − t³ + x₀ with x₀ = 0. x(3) = −27 + 54 − 27 = 0 m.

D. x(1) = −9 + 6 − 1 = −4 m. From t = 0 to 1 the particle moves 4 m in −x; from t = 1 to 3 it moves from −4 m back to 0, another 4 m. Total distance = 8 m.

E. At t = 0.5 s, v = −3.75 m/s and a = 12 − 3 = 9 m/s². Velocity and acceleration have opposite signs, so the particle is slowing down.
